title: Whale Rider
full_review:
Determined to win her grandfather's love and respect, a 12-year-old Maori girl defies his edict that she not learn warrior skills in the evocative tale "Whale Rider" (Newmarket).

The very contemporary retelling of the Maori legend is written and directed by Niki Caro, based on the 1986 best seller by Witi Ihimaera, New Zealand's first published Maori novelist.

Local legend holds that the sea god Paikea arrived in their North Island village of Whangara on the back of a whale. Aging tribal chief Koro (Rawiri Paratene) is distraught when his son's wife dies bearing twins, with the male infant dying as well. Resenting Koro's insensitivity to his baby daughter, the grief-stricken father (Cliff Curtis) gives her the male-only name of Paikea and leaves New Zealand.

Called Pai, the child (Keisha Castle-Hughes) is aware her grandfather wishes her brother had lived instead, but her grandmother (Vicky Haughton) provides the affection her grandfather feels but does not show.

With no male heir available to lead, Koro begins training local boys in the gestures and fighting stances the new leader must possess. Pai surreptitiously practices and excels in the necessary skills, exhibiting a natural leadership lacking in the unmotivated boys around her.

When Pai's father returns for a visit, an ugly flare-up again distances him from his own father and he offers to take Pai back to Germany with him. She is sorely tempted but decides her destiny is to prove herself to her grandfather as the person he is seeking to succeed him.

Despite Koro's refusal to acknowledge her talents, she speaks in beautiful tribute to him at a school ceremony where she has won two top prizes. Apologizing for upsetting his tradition-bound ways, she can hardly get the words out as he has not shown up to hear how much she loves and honors him. Instead, on the way, Koro is sidetracked by a crisis of beached whales that will test the resolve of the entire village -- and trigger a significant change of heart.

Castle-Hughes makes a radiant debut as the loving child whose youth belies her emotional and spiritual maturity. Indeed, her willingness to sacrifice herself for her people is Christ-like, and her ability to forgive her grandfather's many slights deeply touching. Caro orchestrates a remarkable exploration of an ancient culture confronting change during hardscrabble times while pulling together as a community to maintain their sacred ties to nature. Although Pai is specifically battling the tribe's rigid patriarchy and accepted gender bias, the narrative embraces universal themes and evokes intense emotions.

Each in their own way, Paratene and Haughton, as the very differing grandparents, bring a strong presence to their roles and were undoubtedly helpful to 11-year-old Castle-Hughes.
The all-Maori cast and the on-location shooting in the village of Whangara, on New Zealand's east coast, only adds to the cinematic experience. Viewers are sure to notice the exquisitely carved interiors of the tribe's meeting house, but it is the interiors of the spirit of this indigenous people that is so impressively celebrated in "Whale Rider."

Because of a brief sexual and drug-related reference, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
